newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian rebels warn against Western meddling.
newsitem.headline: Algerian rebels warn against Western meddling.

text.p: A militant Algerian fundamentalist group has warned France and other Western nations against meddling in its campaign to topple the Algerian authorities, a French newspaper said on Monday.

The daily Le Monde said it had received a statement from the outlawed Islamic Salvation Army (AIS) accusing Algiers of involvement in "horrible crimes" and warning Western states against aiding the Algerian authorities.
A spokesman for the French Foreign Ministry said he was unaware of the statement but said Paris wanted Algerian domestic matters to be regulated "by the Algerians and for the Algerians".
The warning surfaced during a period of growing violence in Algeria between Moslem rebels and the military-backed authorities.

It also was sent a little over a month after the rush-hour bombing of a Paris commuter train on December 3 in which four people died. French investigators suspect another rebel group, the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) in the Paris train bombing.
The GIA had earlier claimed responsibility for a series of 1995 bombing attacks in France, blaming Paris for propping up the Algerian authorities.

The AIS, one of several Moslem rebel groups vying to transform Algeria into an Islamic republic, is known as the armed wing of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), another fundamentalist group banned in Algeria.

The rebel movement was launched after the authorities cancelled 1992 general elections that the FIS was poised to win. Some 60,000 people, including many civilians and more than 100 foreigners, have died in subsequent violence.
The AIS statement appeared to draw a line between its tactics and those of the GIA, considered the most ruthless of the Moslem rebel groups in Algeria.

It said that using illegal means to achieve a goal was against Moslem law and insisted it was "innocent of all terrorist action which targets innocents who are not involved in the fighting between combattants".
The group said Western aid to the Algerian "putschist regime" was against the interests of the Algerian people, serving only to "increase the oppressors' criminal capacities".
It said Algerian aid should be channeled through private humanitarian groups rather than through Algiers.
